What is the purpose of EXPOSE in a Docke: `EXPOSE` documents which port the container listens on at runtime - it's purely informational/metadata (visible via `docker inspect` and to tools that read it) and does not actually publish the port to the host; you still need `-p` on `docker run` or a `ports:` entry in docker-compose to make the port reachable from outside the container.
What is RUN used for in a Dockerfile?: `RUN` executes a command at image build time and commits the result as a new layer - used for installing packages, compiling code, or any setup that should be baked into the image itself, as opposed to `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT` which define what runs when a container is started from the finished image, not during the build.
How do you expose a FastAPI application: In the Dockerfile: `EXPOSE 8000` (documentation) and `CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]` - critically, uvicorn must bind to `0.0.0.0`, not `127.0.0.1`, since binding to localhost inside the container makes it unreachable from outside the container even with correct port publishing.
How does the application code become ava: The `COPY` (or `ADD`) instruction in the Dockerfile copies source files from the build context on the host into the image's filesystem at build time - for a compiled/dependency-based app, this is typically preceded by copying just the dependency manifest (requirements.txt/package.json) and installing dependencies first, then copying the rest of the source, so Docker's layer cache can skip reinstalling dependencies when only source code changes.
What command starts the application insi: The Dockerfile's `CMD` or `ENTRYPOINT` instruction, executed automatically when a container is started from the image (e.g. `CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]`) - `ENTRYPOINT` is used when the container should always run as a fixed executable (with `CMD` supplying default arguments to it), while `CMD` alone is fully overridable at `docker run` time.
How do you publish a Docker container po: `docker run -p <host-port>:<container-port> <image>` maps a port on the host machine to a port inside the container, making the containerized service reachable via the host's IP/port - without `-p`, the container's port is only reachable from other containers on the same Docker network, not from the host or outside.
What is the purpose of docker run -p?: It creates a port forwarding rule from the host to the container, allowing traffic sent to the specified host port to reach the service listening on the container's internal port - this is what actually makes a containerized web service accessible to a browser or client outside the Docker host, complementing the Dockerfile's `EXPOSE` (which only documents intent).
What are the different types of Kubernet: ClusterIP (internal-only, default), NodePort (opens a static port on every node), LoadBalancer (provisions an external cloud load balancer), and ExternalName (DNS CNAME alias to an external name) - the choice depends on whether the service needs to be reached from inside the cluster only, from outside via a specific node, or via a full managed external load balancer.
How do you expose an application externa: Use a Service of type LoadBalancer (provisions a cloud load balancer automatically) or, more commonly for HTTP(S) traffic at scale, an Ingress resource behind an Ingress Controller, which lets one external load balancer route to many services based on host/path rules rather than provisioning a separate cloud load balancer per service.
What is the equivalent of Docker port ma: A Kubernetes Service's `port`/`targetPort` combination plays a similar role to Docker's `-p host:container` mapping - the Service exposes a virtual `port` that maps to the actual `targetPort` the container listens on, and (for NodePort/LoadBalancer types) further maps that to a node port or external load balancer port reachable from outside the cluster.
How do containerPort, port, and targetPo: `containerPort` (in the Pod spec) documents what port the container listens on, similar to Dockerfile's EXPOSE - informational for the Pod. `port` (on the Service) is the port other things inside the cluster use to reach the Service. `targetPort` (also on the Service) is the actual port on the Pod that traffic gets forwarded to - `port` and `targetPort` can differ (e.g. Service port 80 forwarding to container port 8000), giving flexibility to present a clean external port while the app listens on whatever port it actually uses.
How do you deploy an application using K: Write YAML manifests for the needed objects (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, etc.) and apply them with `kubectl apply -f <file-or-directory>` - Kubernetes reconciles the cluster's actual state to match what's declared, creating, updating, or leaving unchanged each object as needed based on the diff between the manifest and current cluster state.
What is the kubectl apply command?: `kubectl apply` declaratively creates or updates resources to match a manifest file - unlike `kubectl create` (which only creates and errors if the resource already exists) or `kubectl replace` (which fully overwrites), `apply` computes a patch of just the differences and merges it, making it safe to re-run repeatedly (idempotent) and the standard choice for CI/CD and GitOps workflows.
After pushing an image to ECR, what is t: Update the Kubernetes Deployment manifest to reference the new image tag (or digest) and apply that change to the cluster (`kubectl apply` or via the CI/CD pipeline's deploy stage) - simply pushing to ECR doesn't change what's running; the cluster only picks up a new image when a Deployment is explicitly updated to point at it.
How do you update the Deployment manifes: Change the `image:` field under the container spec to the new tag/digest (e.g. `myapp:v1.2.3` or the immutable digest), then `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml` (or `kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=myrepo/myapp:v1.2.3` for a quick imperative update) - Kubernetes then performs a rolling update, replacing old Pods with new ones running the updated image.
If the latest image is pushed but the po: If using a mutable tag like `:latest` with `imagePullPolicy: Always`, a rollout restart (`kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>`) forces Kubernetes to pull the image fresh and recreate Pods - but the more reliable practice is always deploying with a unique, immutable tag or digest per build, so Kubernetes detects an actual image change and updates automatically without relying on force-pulling a mutable tag.
Have you worked on Helm charts?: Answer with actual scope - whether you've authored charts from scratch (templates, values.yaml, helpers) or primarily consumed/customized existing public charts by overriding values, and one concrete example of a chart you've worked with, to give an honest calibration for follow-up depth.
Explain an automated deployment pipeline: On merge: build the FastAPI app into a Docker image, run tests and security/dependency scans, push the image (tagged with the commit SHA) to ECR, then update the Kubernetes Deployment manifest's image tag and apply it to EKS (via `kubectl`, Helm, or a GitOps controller like ArgoCD watching the manifests repo) - health checks (readiness probes, a post-deploy smoke test) gate whether the rollout is considered successful, with automatic rollback on failure.
What checks would you perform before dep: Unit and integration tests passing, static code analysis/linting clean, dependency vulnerability scan clear of critical findings, secret scanning confirming no credentials are committed, container image vulnerability scan passing, and a successful build/containerization step - all as required, automated CI gates rather than manual pre-deploy checklist items someone might skip under time pressure.
How would you perform code formatting, l: Formatting/linting via language-specific tools (Black/Flake8 for Python, ESLint/Prettier for JS) run as a pre-commit hook and CI stage; unit testing via the language's test framework (pytest, Jest) with coverage reporting; dependency vulnerability scanning via `pip-audit`/`npm audit`/Snyk; secret scanning via gitleaks/truffleHog on every commit; and container image scanning via Trivy/Grype as a dedicated CI stage after the image builds, each configured to fail the pipeline on findings above a defined severity threshold.
Where would you push the Docker image?: A container registry - Artifact Registry (GCP), ECR (AWS), or Docker Hub for public images - chosen based on which cloud the deployment target lives in for lowest-latency, most cost-efficient pulls, with the registry's own IAM controlling who/what can push and pull images.
How would you deploy the image after pus: Update the Kubernetes Deployment's image reference to the new ECR image URI/tag and apply the change to the EKS cluster - either directly via `kubectl`/Helm from the pipeline, or by updating a GitOps-managed manifests repo and letting ArgoCD/Flux pick up and apply the change, which is the preferred pattern for production for its audit trail and drift detection.
How would you automate the deployment?: Wire the entire sequence (build, scan, push, update manifest, apply/sync) into a CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI) triggered automatically on merge to main, with no manual steps required for a normal deploy - manual intervention should only be a deliberate gate (e.g. a required approval for production), not a routine part of the process.
What is a ConfigMap?: A Kubernetes object storing non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs or config files, which can be injected into Pods as environment variables or mounted as files - it decouples configuration from the container image so the same image can be reused across environments with different config.
What is stored inside a ConfigMap?: Non-sensitive application configuration - feature flags, URLs of other services, log levels, or entire configuration files (e.g. an nginx.conf or application.yaml) - anything you'd be comfortable viewing in plaintext, since ConfigMaps have no encryption or special access restriction beyond standard RBAC.
What are Kubernetes Secrets?: Secrets are similar to ConfigMaps but intended for sensitive data (passwords, API keys, certificates) - stored base64-encoded (not encrypted by default at rest unless encryption at rest is explicitly enabled on the cluster) with tighter expected RBAC around who can read them, and typically layered with a secrets manager integration (External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets) in production rather than relying on base64 alone.
How do you use Secrets inside a pod?: Reference the Secret in the Pod spec either as environment variables (`env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef`) or as a mounted volume (files appear under a mount path, one file per key) - mounted volumes are often preferred since a Secret update propagates to the mounted file without restarting the Pod (though the app needs to watch for the file change), whereas environment variables are fixed at container start.
What is the difference between ConfigMap: Functionally similar (both inject key-value data into Pods), but Secrets are intended for sensitive data and are base64-encoded with tighter expected access controls, while ConfigMaps are plaintext and meant for non-sensitive configuration - the distinction is primarily about intent and access control expectations, not strong built-in encryption (base64 is encoding, not encryption).
How can you expose a service only to use: Use an internal-only load balancer (annotated/configured for internal traffic only, not internet-facing) or keep the Service as ClusterIP/internal Ingress and require access via VPN or a bastion into the private network, combined with restricting the Ingress/LB's firewall rules to your organization's known IP ranges or VPC.
Without using SSO or RBAC, how would you: Network-level controls: an internal load balancer with no public IP, firewall rules/security groups allow-listing only your organization's known CIDR ranges, or requiring connectivity through a VPN/private network path - these restrict at the network layer rather than the identity layer, which is the right approach when SSO/RBAC (identity-layer controls) aren't an option.
Can NetworkPolicy solve this problem?: Partially - NetworkPolicy controls traffic between Pods/namespaces within the cluster (e.g. only allow the frontend namespace to reach the backend namespace), but it doesn't control traffic coming from outside the cluster's network boundary at the internet/organization level - for restricting external user access by IP range, you need the Ingress/load balancer's own firewall/allow-list configuration, not NetworkPolicy, which operates one layer below that.
How would you whitelist an organization': Configure the allow-list at whichever layer terminates external traffic - a cloud load balancer's firewall rule, an Ingress annotation supported by the ingress controller (e.g. nginx-ingress's `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/whitelist-source-range`), or a VPC firewall rule - restricting to only the organization's known public IP ranges or VPN egress IPs.
What is the role of an Internal Load Bal: An internal load balancer only has a private IP, reachable exclusively from within the VPC/private network (or over VPN/Direct Connect into it), never from the public internet - used to expose a service to internal consumers (other internal services, employees over VPN) while keeping it completely unreachable from the open internet, which is more robust than merely relying on firewall rules on a public-facing load balancer.
What is service-to-service authenticatio: The mechanism by which one internal service proves its identity to another before the receiving service trusts and processes its request - common approaches include mutual TLS (both sides present certificates), signed service-account tokens (Kubernetes' own service account JWTs, verified by the receiving service or a sidecar), or API keys/short-lived tokens issued by an internal identity provider.
How do two services communicate securely: Encrypt in transit (mTLS, often via a service mesh like Istio/Linkerd handling certificate issuance and rotation automatically), authenticate each side's identity (service account tokens or mTLS client certificates), and authorize the specific request (the receiving service checks the caller's identity against what it's allowed to do) - a service mesh is the common way to get mTLS and authorization policy applied consistently without every service implementing it individually.
How would an App Service communicate wit: Via a connection string configured in App Service's application settings pointing to the PostgreSQL server's hostname/port, ideally over a private VNet integration/private endpoint rather than the database's public endpoint, with credentials sourced from Azure Key Vault rather than stored in plaintext app settings.
How would you authorize App Service to a: Use Azure AD authentication for PostgreSQL with the App Service's Managed Identity, rather than a static username/password - the Managed Identity is granted the appropriate database role, and PostgreSQL validates an Azure AD token from the App Service instead of a long-lived stored credential, eliminating a static secret that would otherwise need rotation and secure storage.
How do Managed Identities work?: Azure assigns an identity directly to a resource (an App Service, a VM) without any credential you manage - Azure AD handles issuing short-lived tokens to that resource automatically, which the resource uses to authenticate to other Azure services (Key Vault, PostgreSQL, Storage) that trust Azure AD, so there's no service principal secret or key to store, rotate, or leak.
How do you provide Contributor access to: Assign the Contributor role to the App Service's Managed Identity (or to a user/group) scoped to the specific resource group or resource - not at the subscription level - via Azure RBAC (`az role assignment create --assignee <identity> --role Contributor --scope <resource-scope>`), following least-privilege by scoping to only what that identity actually needs to manage.
What is Azure App Service?: A fully managed platform-as-a-service for hosting web applications, REST APIs, and mobile backends without managing the underlying VMs/OS - it handles scaling, patching, and load balancing automatically, supporting multiple language runtimes and deployment methods (Git, container images, CI/CD integration).
What is App Service used for?: Hosting web applications and APIs where you want managed infrastructure (automatic scaling, built-in load balancing, easy deployment slots for staging/production swaps) without operating VMs or Kubernetes yourself - it trades some flexibility for significantly lower operational overhead, similar in positioning to GCP App Engine or AWS Elastic Beanstalk.
How do applications hosted on App Servic: Via a connection string in App Service's configuration (ideally referencing Key Vault rather than storing the raw string), over VNet integration for private connectivity to the database rather than its public endpoint, and using Managed Identity-based authentication where the database supports it instead of static credentials.
How comfortable are you with API develop: Give an honest, specific answer naming the frameworks/patterns you've used (REST with FastAPI/Flask, gRPC, GraphQL), what you've actually designed versus consumed, and one concrete example of an API you built end-to-end (including how you handled versioning, auth, and error handling) to substantiate the claim.
Have you built APIs yourself?: Answer with a specific example - the framework used, the purpose of the API, key design decisions (authentication method, versioning strategy, error response format), and how it was deployed/operated - a concrete example is far more convincing than a general yes/no.
How would you build an observability nam: A dedicated `observability` (or `monitoring`) namespace hosting the shared stack - Prometheus/Grafana (often via the kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart), a log aggregator (Loki or an ELK stack), and an OpenTelemetry Collector - isolated from application namespaces for clear ownership and resource accounting, with RBAC scoped so it can read metrics/logs cluster-wide without application teams needing access to its internals.
Which services would you use for metrics: Metrics: Prometheus (scraping) with Grafana for visualization. Logs: Loki (pairs naturally with Grafana) or an ELK/EFK stack for centralized log aggregation. Traces: an OpenTelemetry Collector receiving instrumented trace data, exported to a tracing backend like Jaeger or Tempo - all three pillars typically converge in Grafana as the single visualization layer even though the underlying storage backends differ.
How would you integrate Grafana?: Deploy Grafana (via the kube-prometheus-stack chart or standalone) and add each backend (Prometheus, Loki, Tempo/Jaeger) as a data source in Grafana's configuration, then build or import dashboards querying across them - Grafana's strength is unifying multiple backend data sources into one consistent dashboarding and alerting UI rather than needing a separate tool per signal type.
What exactly is OpenTelemetry?: OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral, open standard (APIs, SDKs, and a Collector) for generating and exporting observability data - metrics, logs, and traces - from instrumented applications. It decouples instrumentation from the backend you send data to, so you can switch or add backends (Prometheus, Datadog, Jaeger) later without re-instrumenting application code.
OpenTelemetry is only a collector; what: The OpenTelemetry Collector receives, processes, and exports telemetry data but doesn't store or visualize it itself - you still need actual backends: Prometheus or a metrics store for metrics, Loki/Elasticsearch for logs, and Jaeger/Tempo for traces, with Grafana (or the backend's own UI) providing visualization on top.
How would Grafana connect to those servi: Each backend (Prometheus, Loki, Tempo/Jaeger) is added as a Grafana data source with its connection URL and any required auth, after which Grafana can query all of them from a single dashboard - correlating, for example, a metric spike with corresponding logs and a trace from the same time window, side by side.
Suppose millions of users access your AP: Horizontally scale stateless API Pods via HPA on request-based custom metrics (not just CPU), spread across multiple node pools/availability zones for resilience, front with a CDN and caching layer (Redis, or edge caching) to absorb repeat read traffic before it hits the API at all, use cluster autoscaling to add node capacity automatically, and ensure the database tier (often the actual bottleneck at this scale) is separately scaled via read replicas/sharding rather than assuming Kubernetes autoscaling alone solves database-tier load.
How would you determine your scaling str: Load test to find the actual bottleneck first (CPU-bound, memory-bound, or downstream-dependency-bound) rather than guessing, then choose the scaling signal that matches (request concurrency/queue depth for I/O-bound APIs, CPU for compute-bound work), and set HPA/cluster autoscaler thresholds with headroom for traffic spikes given that scale-up isn't instantaneous (new pods/nodes take time to become ready).
How would you estimate the number of pod: Start from a per-pod capacity benchmark from load testing (e.g. one pod sustainably handles X requests/second at acceptable latency), divide expected peak traffic by that per-pod capacity to get a baseline replica count, add headroom for traffic spikes and rolling deploys (so a deploy doesn't reduce available capacity below what's needed), and let HPA handle the ongoing adjustment around that baseline rather than hardcoding a fixed replica count.
How would you perform load testing?: Define realistic scenarios matching actual traffic patterns (not just a flat ramp), use a tool to generate load against a staging/pre-production environment sized like production, and measure the metrics that matter (p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, and the point where the system's behavior degrades) rather than just a single throughput number - identify the actual bottleneck (app, database, network) the test reveals, not just confirm a target number was hit.
Can you generate 5,000 requests per seco: Yes, with the right tooling and enough load-generator capacity - a single machine running a simple tool may not reach that rate itself (the load generator can become the bottleneck), so distributed load generation (multiple load-generator instances, or a managed service like Locust in distributed mode or a cloud load-testing service) is typically needed to reliably sustain 5,000+ RPS without the test tool itself skewing results.
Which load-testing tools would you use?: k6 or Locust for scriptable, code-based load tests integrated into CI/CD; Apache JMeter for a GUI-driven, broader protocol-support option; and Vegeta or hey for quick simple HTTP load checks - the choice depends on whether the test needs to be a repeatable, version-controlled part of the pipeline (k6/Locust) or a one-off ad hoc check.
